clinicalPearls: Occurs when an oxidising drug or chemical converts haemoglobin iron to the ferric state, forming methaemoglobin which cannot carry oxygen
Common precipitants include topical/local anaesthetics (benzocaine, prilocaine), dapsone, nitrites and nitrates, and aniline dyes
Classic clue is cyanosis that does NOT improve with supplemental oxygen, with a normal arterial oxygen tension
Blood appears characteristically chocolate-brown and does not redden on exposure to air
Pulse oximetry is unreliable, often reading around the mid-80s regardless of true saturation; co-oximetry is required
Severity ranges from asymptomatic through headache and fatigue to obtundation, arrhythmia and death as levels rise
Methylthioninium chloride (methylene blue) is the specific antidote for significant or symptomatic cases
reference.pathophysiology: Haemoglobin normally contains iron in the ferrous state, which binds oxygen. Oxidising agents convert some iron to the ferric (methaemoglobin) form, which cannot bind oxygen and also shifts the oxygen affinity of the remaining ferrous haem, impairing oxygen delivery further. Endogenous cytochrome-b5 reductase normally reconverts methaemoglobin, but this capacity is overwhelmed by oxidant stress. Methylthioninium chloride acts as an artificial electron acceptor via NADPH-methaemoglobin reductase to accelerate reduction back to functional haemoglobin; it is ineffective and potentially harmful in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital methaemoglobinaemia (cytochrome-b5 reductase deficiency or HbM)
Shock or poor peripheral perfusion causing cyanosis
additionalInvestigations: Co-oximetry to measure the methaemoglobin fraction
Arterial blood gas (oxygen tension typically normal)
Full blood count and assessment for haemolysis
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status before giving methylthioninium chloride
redFlags: Cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen with a high methaemoglobin fraction
Coexisting anaemia amplifying the impact on oxygen delivery
Ongoing exposure to the causative oxidant
reference.prognosis: Most cases respond rapidly to removal of the oxidant and, where indicated, methylthioninium chloride; severe or unrecognised cases, or those with G6PD deficiency limiting antidote use, carry higher risk.
pitfalls: Trusting a normal-looking pulse oximeter reading, which is unreliable in methaemoglobinaemia
Giving methylthioninium chloride in G6PD deficiency, which can precipitate haemolysis and is ineffective
Missing the diagnosis when cyanosis fails to respond to oxygen
Overlooking topical anaesthetic sprays as a common precipitant
